content: 1. The use of fixed-dose combination NRTI backbones is strongly recommended as the preferred approach for antiretroviral therapy (ART), supported by moderate-quality evidence. 2. Heat-stable fixed-dose combinations of ATV/r and LPV/r are the preferred boosted protease inhibitor (PI) options for second-line ART, with strong recommendations based on moderate-quality evidence. 3. A heat-stable fixed-dose combination of DRV/r can be considered as an alternative boosted PI option for second-line ART, though this is a conditional recommendation supported by low-quality evidence. 4. A combination of RAL plus LPV/r may also be used as an alternative second-line ART regimen, with a conditional recommendation and low-quality evidence. 5. Viral load testing should be performed early after initiating ART (within 6 months), at 12 months, and then at least every 12 months to detect treatment failure. 6. If viral load testing is not routinely available, CD4 count and clinical monitoring should be used to diagnose treatment failure, with targeted viral load testing to confirm viral failure where possible. 7. WHO defines individuals as stable on ART if they have been on ART for at least one year, have no current illnesses or pregnancy, demonstrate good understanding of lifelong adherence, and show evidence of treatment success (two consecutive viral load measurements below 1000 copies/mL). 8. For service delivery recommendations, an additional criterion is the absence of adverse drug reactions requiring regular monitoring, though this is not relevant to the current recommendation. 9. For children under 3 years of age who fail a first-line LPV/r-based regimen, switching to a RAL-based second-line regimen is conditionally recommended, though evidence quality is very low. 10. For children older than 3 years who fail a first-line LPV/r-based regimen, switching to a second-line regimen containing two NRTIs plus EFV or RAL is conditionally recommended, with very low-quality evidence. 11. After failure of a first-line NNRTI-based regimen, children should switch to a boosted PI-based regimen, with LPV/r or ATV/r as the preferred options (conditional recommendation, very low-quality evidence). 12. For second-line ART after failure of a first-line regimen containing ABC or TDF + 3TC (or FTC), the preferred NRTI backbone is AZT + 3TC (strong recommendation, low-quality evidence). 13. National programs should develop policies for third-line ART, which should include new drugs with minimal risk of cross-resistance to previously used regimens, such as INSTIs, second-generation NNRTIs, and PIs (conditional recommendation, low-quality evidence). 14. Patients on a failing second-line regimen with no new ARV options should continue with a tolerated regimen (conditional recommendation, very low-quality evidence). 15. Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis is recommended for adults (including pregnant women) with severe or advanced HIV clinical disease (WHO stage 3 or 4) and/or a CD4 count ≤350 cells/mm³ (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). 16. In settings with high prevalence of malaria and/or severe bacterial infections, co-trimoxazole prophylaxis should be initiated regardless of CD4 count or WHO stage (conditional recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). 17. Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis may be discontinued in adults with HIV who are clinically stable on ART, with evidence of immune recovery and viral suppression (conditional recommendation, low-quality evidence). 18. In high-prevalence settings for malaria and/or severe bacterial infections, co-trimoxazole prophylaxis should be continued regardless of CD4 count or WHO clinical stage (conditional recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). 19. Routine co-trimoxazole prophylaxis should be given to all HIV-infected patients with active TB disease regardless of CD4 count (strong recommendation, high-quality evidence). 20. Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis is recommended for infants, children, and adolescents with HIV, irrespective of clinical and immune conditions, with priority given to children under 5 years old and those with severe or advanced HIV clinical disease (WHO stage 3 or 4) and/or CD4 ≤350 cells/mm³ (strong recommendation, high-quality evidence). 21. In settings with high prevalence of malaria and/or severe bacterial infections, co-trimoxazole prophylaxis should be continued until adulthood, irrespective of ART provision (conditional recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). 22. In low-prevalence settings for malaria and bacterial infections, co-trimoxazole prophylaxis may be discontinued for children aged 5 years and older who are clinically stable and/or virally suppressed on ART for at least 6 months and with a CD4 count >350 cells/mm³ (strong recommendation, very low-quality evidence). 23. Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis is recommended for HIV-exposed infants from 4 to 6 weeks of age and should be continued until HIV infection is excluded by an age-appropriate HIV test after complete cessation of breastfeeding (strong recommendation, very low-quality evidence). 24. Xpert MTB/RIF should be used as the initial diagnostic test for adults and children suspected of having HIV-associated TB or multidrug-resistant TB, rather than conventional microscopy, culture, and drug susceptibility testing (strong recommendation, high-quality evidence for adults; very low-quality evidence for children). 25. Xpert MTB/RIF should be used in preference to conventional microscopy and culture for cerebrospinal fluid specimens from patients suspected of having TB meningitis (strong recommendation, very low-quality evidence). 26. Xpert MTB/RIF may be used as a replacement test for conventional methods (e.g., microscopy, culture, or histopathology) for testing specific non-respiratory specimens (e.g., lymph nodes and other tissues) from patients suspected of having extrapulmonary TB (conditional recommendation, very low-quality evidence). 27. Urine lateral flow (LF)-LAM should not be used for TB diagnosis in people living with HIV except in specific cases, such as those with CD4 counts ≤100 cells/mm³ or those who are seriously ill (conditional recommendation, low-quality evidence). 28. ART is recommended for all patients with HIV and drug-resistant TB requiring second-line antituberculosis drugs, irrespective of CD4 count, as early as possible (within the first 8 weeks) following initiation of antituberculosis treatment (strong recommendation, very low-quality evidence). 29. For cryptococcal disease, prompt lumbar puncture with measurement of CSF opening pressure and rapid CSF cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) assay or rapid serum CrAg testing is the preferred diagnostic approach (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). 30. Routine antifungal primary prophylaxis for cryptococcal disease in HIV-infected individuals with CD4 counts <100 cells/mm³ who are CrAg-negative or have unknown CrAg status is not recommended prior to ART initiation unless a prolonged delay in ART initiation is likely (strong recommendation, high-quality evidence). 31. Routine CrAg screening in ART-naïve adults, followed by pre-emptive antifungal therapy if CrAg-positive, may be considered in populations with a high prevalence (>3%) of cryptococcal antigenaemia (conditional recommendation, low-quality evidence). 32. Routine CrAg screening in ART-naïve adolescents and children with pre-emptive antifungal therapy if CrAg-positive is not recommended (conditional recommendation, low-quality evidence). 33. For the induction phase of treatment in HIV-infected individuals with cryptococcal disease, a two-week antifungal regimen is recommended.
